headline: Scotts Miracle-Gro values Vireo Growth stake at $81.7M in 10-K
dek: Scotts Miracle-Gro's fiscal 2026 10-K shows a $14.7 million unrealized loss on the Vireo Growth shares and warrants it took for selling Hawthorne in April.
key_points: Scotts Miracle-Gro's annual report for the year to 30 September 2026 puts its Vireo Growth shares and warrants at $81.7 million, according to The Marijuana Herald's reading of the filing.
The filing confirms Scotts received 7.1 million Vireo shares, about 14% of Vireo at closing, plus a five-year warrant for 2.7 million shares at $25.50, when it sold Hawthorne on 8 April.
Scotts booked a $14.7 million unrealized loss on the Vireo securities in fiscal 2026 and a $106.2 million pre-tax loss on the Hawthorne sale.
On our arithmetic the shares are valued near $9.59 each, well below the warrants' $25.50 strike.
body: The lawn and garden giant that once bet heavily on cannabis growers now holds its cannabis exposure as a stake in a multistate operator. Scotts Miracle-Gro's annual report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended 30 September 2026, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, shows the company carrying its investment in Vireo Growth as a non-core holding at fair value, and booking a $14.7 million unrealized loss on it for the year.

According to The Marijuana Herald's reading of the filing, the Vireo shares were worth $68.1 million and the warrants $13.6 million at 30 September, for a combined $81.7 million, slightly up from $81.3 million at the end of June and down from an initial value of $96.4 million. We confirmed the deal terms and the unrealized loss in the 10-K itself; the valuation breakdown is as reported by the Herald.
## How Scotts ended up owning part of Vireo

The stake is what remains of Hawthorne Gardening Company, the hydroponics and cultivation-supply business Scotts built during the first wave of legal cannabis. The 10-K says Scotts completed the sale of Hawthorne to Vireo on 8 April 2026. In return it received 7.1 million Vireo common shares, which the filing says were about 14% of Vireo's outstanding shares at closing, and a five-year warrant to buy another 2.7 million shares at $25.50 each. Those numbers reflect a 30-for-1 share consolidation Vireo completed on 5 June 2026.

Scotts also agreed to supply Vireo with up to $20 million of manufacturing services at no charge over two years. The filing records a pre-tax loss of $106.2 million on the Hawthorne sale in fiscal 2026, part of a $91.0 million total loss from discontinued operations.

The Herald reports that the shares are held through an entity called Good Dog Holdings LLC, and that The Hawthorne Collective received another 400,000 Vireo shares linked to Vireo's 9 November acquisition of FLUENT, in which Hawthorne had held about a quarter. We did not find those details in the part of the filing we reviewed.
> Scotts no longer sells picks and shovels to cannabis growers; it owns a slice of one, and its results now move with an MSO's share price.

Two simple calculations put the valuation in context. First, $68.1 million spread over 7.1 million shares works out to about $9.59 a share. That is well under half the warrants' $25.50 strike price, which explains why the warrants carry a value of only $13.6 million despite covering 2.7 million shares: they are worth something only if Vireo's stock more than doubles within their five-year life.

Second, the drop from the initial $96.4 million to $81.7 million is about 15%, in a year in which Vireo grew quickly by acquisition. As we reported on 10 November, Vireo's third-quarter revenue rose 177% to $253.7 million and its annualized revenue passed $1 billion, helped by deals for C21 Investments' Nevada stores and PharmaCann's Colorado retail assets. Vireo has since closed the FLUENT deal, which we covered on 9 November, and has a shareholder vote on its Planet 13 Holdings acquisition scheduled for 10 December.

The gap between fast revenue growth and a falling equity value is common across U.S. cannabis stocks, which remain mostly on Canadian exchanges and U.S. over-the-counter markets and still carry federal tax and banking burdens despite this year's partial rescheduling for state medical programs.

For Scotts the Vireo stake is small next to its balance sheet. The 10-K shows $2,039.0 million of debt outstanding at 30 September, with $1,220.2 million available under its credit agreement, and a leverage ratio of 3.89 against a permitted maximum of 5.00. The company bought back $25.0 million of stock in fiscal 2026 under a $500 million programme authorised in December 2025.

The filing also records leadership change. Nathan E. Baxter succeeded James Hagedorn as chief executive on 26 June 2026, and Hagedorn left the board. Hagedorn had been the public face of Scotts' cannabis push. The Hagedorn Partnership still owned about 23% of Scotts' common shares as of 20 November, according to the filing. The 10-K also notes an agreement in principle reached on 16 November to resolve the long-running securities class action against the company.

Vireo shareholders vote on the Planet 13 deal on 10 December; if it and Vireo's other announced deals close, Vireo has said it would run about 270 dispensaries in 15 states. Vireo's guidance calls for fourth-quarter revenue of $250 million to $265 million. Scotts' next quarterly report will show whether the fair value of its Vireo shares moved with that growth, and any future sale of the stake would have to be disclosed in its filings.
